the normalized tool under test (name, description, inputSchema, annotations) + its TokenBreakdown from mcp_tool_scans
the server scan aggregate (total_tools, total_tokens, total_raw_bytes, tools[]) from mcp_scans / mcp_tool_scans
the per-model object from data/**/*.json (== all-models.json[].detail)
runtime execution data from tool_executions / run_steps (live session only)
aggregate across ALL connected servers in the environment (sum of their scans) + built-in/model tools — the scope where vendor/host caps actually bind

execution_modes.static_connection: Connected to the server + tools/list (and resources/list, prompts/list). NO tool execution, NO server source code. == the existing discovery scan.
execution_modes.single_tool_exec: Execute ONE tool once (tools/call) and inspect the request/response. == the existing tool playground + runtime token accounting. No multi-turn.
execution_modes.live_session: Requires a multi-turn, monitored agent session. BACKLOG — depends on the live-session monitoring now being built.

excluded_from_automation.concern: OAuth 2.1 / token audience / no token pass-through

excluded_from_automation.reason: cannot be inferred from the tool schema; needs source
transport internals; only HTTPS scheme is observable from config
subjective design judgement; best surfaced via the live-session effectiveness eval, not a static check

scoring.cell_score: 100 * sum(weight_s * verdict_value) / sum(weight_s) over APPLICABLE tests (na excluded)
scoring.gate: any blocker-severity test with verdict=fail forces the cell to red/incompatible regardless of score

tests.user_facing_name: Single server's tool count vs the model's cap
tests.what_it_does: Checks whether THIS ONE server's tool count alone would exceed the model's per-request cap. This is a single-server upper-bound check; the binding limit across all connected servers is ENV_AGGREGATE_TOOL_COUNT.

applies_to.models_note: Only models/hosts with a published hard cap: Gemini 512, OpenAI 128, Mistral 128, Grok 200, GitHub Copilot 128, M365 Copilot 10. NA for Anthropic and open-weight (use SERVER_TOOL_COUNT_CONTEXT instead).

verdict_bands.na: hard cap not documented for this model

tests.recommendation: Split the server, disable unused tools, or enable tool-search/deferred loading so fewer than the cap are presented at once. On Gemini the 512 functionDeclarations cap is the wall; on OpenAI/Grok/Mistral trim to the 128/200 limit.

impact.what_happens: The API rejects the entire request (HTTP 400) once tool count exceeds the model's hard cap.

rules.consequence: If this single server alone exceeds the per-request cap, the request fails before any other server is added.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s per-request cap is {tools_mcp.max_tools_hard} tools; a single server exceeding it fails the request outright — and the combined total across servers is checked by ENV_AGGREGATE_TOOL_COUNT.

rules.consequence: No fixed per-request count cap, so one server cannot be rejected on count here; the binding ceilings are the aggregate catalog max and the ~40 selection cliff.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} has no fixed per-request tool-count cap, so a single server cannot be rejected on count here; the binding limits are AGGREGATE (see ENV_AGGREGATE_TOOL_COUNT) and the ~40 selection cliff (SERVER_TOOL_COUNT_PRACTICAL).

tests.user_facing_name: Tool count within the reliable-selection range
tests.what_it_does: Checks the tool count against the empirical point where tool-selection accuracy degrades (well below any hard cap). More tools than this and the model starts picking the wrong tool. The ~30-50 selection cliff is across ALL tools in context, not one server — evaluate the combined set via ENV_AGGREGATE_TOOL_COUNT.

applies_to.models_note: Universal. Uses the model's practical value where known (~30-50 frontier, 5-20 small open-weight); falls back to 40.

tests.recommendation: Group or gate tools so the active set stays under the practical ceiling. Consider a router/loader tool, tool-search deferral, or per-task tool subsets. Small open-weight models (Phi, Gemma) need especially short tool lists.

impact.what_happens: The model increasingly calls the wrong tool (or none) as the list grows past the selection cliff.

rules.consequence: Past the cliff the model increasingly mis-selects tools.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s reliable-selection cliff is ~{tools_mcp.max_tools_practical} tools; beyond it selection accuracy drops (small models degrade hardest).

rules.consequence: No published cliff; assume ~40 for frontier, fewer for small models.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} publishes no selection-cliff figure; use ~40 (frontier) as a default — small models degrade well before that.

tests.user_facing_name: Tools physically fit the context window
tests.what_it_does: For models with NO vendor hard cap (Anthropic, all open-weight), computes the structural ceiling = how many tools of this server's average definition size fit in the window with output headroom, and checks the server stays under it. Single-server view; the window is shared, so the binding fit-check across all servers is ENV_AGGREGATE_FOOTPRINT.

applies_to.models_note: Primary for models where max_tools_hard is null; informative for all. This is the 'max tools possible' number for uncapped models.

tests.recommendation: Reduce per-tool definition size (shorter descriptions, leaner schemas) or raise the serving context (self-host: --max-model-len). The derived ceiling scales with the window, so a larger-window model lifts this limit.

impact.what_happens: Tool definitions crowd the window, leaving too little room for the conversation; eventual truncation.

rules.consequence: On a tiny window the structural tool-fit ceiling is so low that this server's definitions can crowd out the conversation entirely.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window leaves almost no room once tool definitions are loaded; the derived fit-ceiling (in the verdict bands) is small, so a modest server can overflow it.

rules.consequence: A mid window gives a finite fit-ceiling; exceeding it leaves too little room for the conversation.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window caps how many average-sized tools physically fit; past the derived ceiling the conversation gets squeezed.

rules.consequence: A large window absorbs many tools; the fit-ceiling is high, so this is mostly a per-call cost concern.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window fits a large tool set; the derived ceiling is generous, so impact is mainly per-call cost unless the server is enormous.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool-definition footprint vs context window
tests.what_it_does: The headline footprint test: what share of the model's context window the server's tool definitions consume before any user message. High shares starve the conversation. Single-server view; the window is shared across servers, so the binding share is ENV_AGGREGATE_FOOTPRINT.

applies_to.models_note: All models. Token total should be recounted with the model's tool shape (see SERVER_TOOL_SHAPE_PROFILE).

tests.extends_existing: optimize.ts huge (generalized to a per-model window share)
tests.recommendation: Trim tool definitions or pick a larger-window model. The same server is trivial on a 1M-window model and crippling on Phi-4 (16K). Enable prompt caching so the static footprint is paid once.

impact.what_happens: A large static footprint is re-sent every call and starves the conversation; on small windows it overflows.

rules.consequence: On a tiny window a heavy tool footprint alone can prevent the conversation from fitting.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window is small; a heavy footprint can overflow it before the user speaks — the verdict bands carry the actual share.

rules.consequence: A mid window means the footprint meaningfully crowds context and adds per-call cost.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window makes a large footprint a real drag on context and cost.

rules.consequence: On a large window the footprint is a minor cost concern, not a fit problem.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window absorbs typical footprints; impact is mostly per-call cost, but a very high share (>=50%) still warns/fails via the verdict bands.

tests.user_facing_name: Serialized tools fit the request size limit
tests.what_it_does: Checks the serialized tool-definitions payload against the API's max request size (a byte/token limit separate from the token window). The request carries ALL connected servers' tool definitions, so the real payload is the aggregate, not one server.

threshold.computed: normalize threshold to bytes: value*1048576 when unit=='MB'; when unit=='tokens' (M365) compare the tool-token footprint, not raw bytes

applies_to.models_note: Where documented: Anthropic 32 MB, Gemini 100 MB, M365 Copilot 4096-token plugin budget. NA elsewhere.

tests.recommendation: Rarely hit by tool definitions alone, but large embedded schemas/examples can. Move bulky reference data out of inputSchema; for M365 Copilot keep the plugin within its 4096-token I/O budget.

impact.what_happens: The serialized request exceeds the API's max payload size and is rejected.

rules.consequence: A serialized payload over the documented cap is rejected before any model work happens.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} caps the request payload at {tools_mcp.max_request_size}; tool definitions rarely hit it, but bulky embedded schemas/examples can — and then the request hard-fails (M365 Copilot's budget is in tokens, not bytes, and is checked as a footprint).

rules.consequence: No documented request-size cap; the binding ceiling is the context window instead.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} documents no request-size cap, so this server cannot be rejected on payload size here; the binding ceiling is the context window — see SERVER_DEFINITION_FOOTPRINT.

tests.user_facing_name: Total tools across all servers within the host client's cap
tests.what_it_does: Sums tools across ALL connected servers and checks the total against the selected host's aggregate cap (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100, VS Code 128). This is an aggregate/client limit, not per-server.

applies_to.models_note: Requires a target client. Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100, VS Code/GitHub Copilot 128, ChatGPT 128.

tests.recommendation: In Cursor keep active tools under ~35 (tools beyond 40 are silently dropped). Use a tool-hub/proxy, disable servers you are not using, or switch to a host with deferral.

impact.what_happens: The host silently drops tools beyond its cap; the model never sees them.

rules.consequence: Tools beyond the host's aggregate cap are silently dropped — the model never sees them, so calls to them simply fail to fire.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} under the selected host enforces an aggregate cap of {cross.clients.<target>.max_tools} tools; everything past it is silently dropped (e.g. Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100, VS Code/ChatGPT 128) — a quiet correctness hit, not a hard error.

tests.user_facing_name: No duplicate tool names
tests.what_it_does: Checks that no two tools share a name within the server (and, with namespacing on, across connected servers) — duplicates are rejected or silently shadowed.

applies_to.models_note: All models/hosts.

tests.recommendation: Rename colliding tools. When connecting multiple MCP servers, confirm the host's namespacing prevents cross-server collisions.

impact.what_happens: Duplicate names are rejected, or one tool silently shadows the other and calls hit the wrong tool.

tests.user_facing_name: Namespaced tool names stay within length limit
tests.what_it_does: Hosts prefix MCP tool names with the server name (e.g. mcp__myserver__toolName). Checks the prefixed length against the model's tool-name cap, which the raw name can pass but the namespaced name fails.

applies_to.models_note: Most relevant on OpenAI/Anthropic (64). Falls back to 64 as the common limit.

tests.recommendation: Shorten tool names or the server handle. Budget for the host's prefix (often 10-20 chars) against the 64-char cap.

impact.what_happens: After the host adds its server prefix the name exceeds the cap and the tool/request is rejected.

rules.consequence: Once the host adds its server-name prefix the combined name exceeds the cap and the tool/request is rejected.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} caps tool names at {tools_mcp.max_tool_name_len} characters; the host prefix (mcp__<server>__) eats into that budget, so an otherwise-fine name can fail once namespaced.

rules.consequence: No documented name-length cap, so the namespaced name will not be rejected here — but it may on stricter providers.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} documents no tool-name length cap, so a long namespaced name will not fail here; it remains a portability risk on providers that cap names at 64 (OpenAI/Anthropic).

tests.user_facing_name: Resources & prompts context impact
tests.what_it_does: Flags that the server also exposes MCP resources and/or prompts, whose reads/templates land in the window as input tokens on top of tool definitions and can dwarf them.

applies_to.models_note: Informational; applies to any server exposing resources/prompts. Neither is spec-capped (cursor-paginated).

verdict_bands.pass: no resources/prompts, or sizes within budget

tests.recommendation: Account for resource-read and prompt-template tokens in the session budget, not just tool definitions. Prefer paginated/summarized resource reads to avoid dumping large payloads into context.

impact.what_happens: Resource reads / prompt templates add input tokens the footprint estimate ignored, inflating context and cost.

tests.user_facing_name: Total tools across all servers within the model's cap
tests.what_it_does: Sums the tools of ALL connected MCP servers (plus built-in/model tools) and checks the total against the model/host AGGREGATE cap — the limit that actually binds (Claude 10k catalog, OpenAI 128, Gemini 512, Cursor 40). This is the real tool-count gate; SERVER_TOOL_COUNT_HARD is only a single-server upper bound.

applies_to.models_note: Aggregate cap = max_tools_hard (OpenAI 128, Gemini 512, Mistral 128, Grok 200) else max_total_tools (Claude 10k catalog w/ tool search). For a target host use cross.clients.<target>.max_tools (Cursor 40, Desktop 100).

tests.recommendation: Trim the active server set, disable unused tools, or enable tool-search/deferral so the COMBINED tool count across all connected servers stays under the cap. The cap is an environment-wide budget shared by every server.

impact.what_happens: Once the combined tool count across all connected servers exceeds the aggregate cap, the request is rejected or tools are silently dropped.

rules.consequence: Combined tools beyond the per-request cap are rejected.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s aggregate per-request cap is {tools_mcp.max_tools_hard} tools; the sum across all connected servers must stay under it.

rules.consequence: Combined tools beyond the catalog max can't be loaded.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s aggregate ceiling is {tools_mcp.max_total_tools} tools (catalog, with tool search); the combined set across servers must fit.

rules.consequence: No documented aggregate count cap; bound by the context window and the ~40 selection cliff across all servers.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} has no documented model-level aggregate count cap; the combined set is bound by the {context.context_window_tokens}-token window and the ~40 selection cliff — and under a host like Cursor (~40) or Claude Desktop (~100) that host cap binds first (see SERVER_CLIENT_TOOL_CAP).

tests.user_facing_name: Combined tool footprint across all servers vs context window
tests.what_it_does: Sums the tool-definition tokens of ALL connected servers (+ built-ins) and checks the share of the model's context window. The window is shared by every server, so this aggregate share — not any single server's — is what starves the conversation.

applies_to.models_note: All models. Recount each server's tools in the model's tool shape before summing.

tests.recommendation: Reduce the COMBINED footprint: fewer active servers, leaner definitions, prompt caching, or a larger-window model. The window budget is shared across every connected server.

impact.what_happens: The combined tool definitions of all servers crowd the shared window, starving the conversation; on small windows it overflows before the first message.

rules.consequence: On a tiny window the combined footprint alone can prevent the conversation from fitting.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window is small; a heavy footprint can overflow it before the user speaks — the verdict bands carry the actual share.

rules.consequence: A mid window means the combined footprint meaningfully crowds context and adds per-call cost.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window makes the combined footprint a real drag on context and cost.

rules.consequence: On a large window the combined footprint is mostly a per-call cost concern.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window absorbs typical footprints; impact is mostly per-call cost, but a very high share (>=50%) still warns/fails via the verdict bands.

tests.user_facing_name: Combined request payload across all servers within the API limit
tests.what_it_does: Sums the serialized tool definitions of ALL connected servers and checks against the API's max request size (Anthropic 32MB, Gemini 100MB). The request carries every server's tools, so this combined payload is what the limit governs.

threshold.computed: normalize MB->bytes (x1048576); skip token-unit budgets (those are footprint, not payload)

applies_to.models_note: Where a request-size cap is documented: Anthropic 32MB, Gemini 100MB. NA elsewhere.

tests.recommendation: Move bulky schemas/examples out of tool definitions; with many servers the COMBINED payload — not one server — is what hits the cap.

impact.what_happens: The combined serialized tool definitions of all servers exceed the API's max payload and the request is rejected.

rules.consequence: Combined payload beyond the cap is rejected.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s max request payload is {tools_mcp.max_request_size}; the combined definitions of all servers must fit (rarely hit unless schemas embed bulk data).

rules.consequence: No documented request-size cap; bound by the context window instead.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} documents no request-size cap; the binding ceiling is the context window — see ENV_AGGREGATE_FOOTPRINT.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool name length
tests.what_it_does: Checks a single tool's name length against the model's tool-name character cap.

applies_to.models_note: OpenAI 64, Anthropic 64. NA where undocumented (Gemini, xAI, Mistral, open-weight).

tests.recommendation: Rename the tool to fit the cap (64 chars on OpenAI/Anthropic), remembering the host adds a server-name prefix.

impact.what_happens: The tool name exceeds the model's name cap and the request is rejected.

rules.consequence: A name longer than the cap is rejected at request time.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} caps tool names at {tools_mcp.max_tool_name_len} characters; a longer name fails the request.

rules.consequence: No documented name-length cap; over-length names are a portability risk, not a failure here.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} documents no tool-name length cap, so this will not fail here — but it is a portability risk on stricter providers (OpenAI/Anthropic cap names at 64); see TOOL_NAME_PATTERN.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool name uses allowed characters
tests.what_it_does: Checks the tool name against the model's required character pattern (e.g. OpenAI ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$). Spaces, dots, or unicode are rejected.

applies_to.models_note: Universal portability lint with the common safe pattern. HARD-FAILS on OpenAI (documented pattern); advisory/warn elsewhere where no pattern is published.

verdict_bands.warn: violates pattern on a model that does not publish one (portability risk)

tests.recommendation: Replace spaces/dots/other characters with underscores or hyphens so the name matches ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$.

impact.what_happens: A name with disallowed characters is rejected where a pattern is enforced; a portability risk elsewhere.

rules.consequence: OpenAI rejects names that violate ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI enforces ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$ on tool names; a non-conforming name fails the request.

rules.consequence: Anthropic enforces the same name regex (max 64 chars).
rules.rationale_template: Anthropic enforces a ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$ tool-name pattern (max 64 chars); a non-conforming name fails the request.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool has a description
tests.what_it_does: Checks the tool has a non-empty description. Without one, the model cannot reliably decide when to call it.

applies_to.models_note: All models.

tests.recommendation: Add a one-line description stating what the tool does and when to use it. This is the single biggest lever on tool-selection accuracy.

impact.what_happens: Without a description the model cannot reliably decide when to call the tool.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool description within length limit
tests.what_it_does: Checks the description against the model's documented maximum description length.

applies_to.models_note: OpenAI ~1024 chars. NA where undocumented.

tests.recommendation: Tighten the description to the documented cap. Move examples/edge-cases into parameter descriptions or external docs.

impact.what_happens: An over-long description is rejected where a cap exists; otherwise it is pure token cost.

rules.consequence: Over-long descriptions are rejected where a cap exists.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} caps tool descriptions (~{tools_mcp.max_tool_description_len} chars); longer ones are rejected.

rules.consequence: No documented cap; length is pure token cost.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} documents no description-length cap; over-long descriptions are a per-call token cost, not a failure.

tests.user_facing_name: Description token cost is reasonable
tests.what_it_does: Flags descriptions whose token cost is disproportionately large, since every tool's description is paid on every request.

applies_to.models_note: All models; thresholds are soft defaults, tune per profile.

tests.recommendation: Shorten verbose descriptions; this cost is multiplied across every call and every tool in the set.

impact.what_happens: A verbose description is paid on every request and across every tool, inflating footprint.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool has a valid input schema
tests.what_it_does: Checks the tool declares a usable inputSchema (object with properties) so arguments can be validated and generated.

applies_to.models_note: All models.

tests.recommendation: Declare an object inputSchema with typed properties; some providers reject non-object roots outright (xAI).

impact.what_happens: Without a usable schema the model can't form valid arguments; some providers reject non-object roots.

rules.consequence: xAI requires the parameters root to be {"type":"object"}; a missing or non-object root returns HTTP 400.
rules.rationale_template: Grok requires a tool's parameters root to be a JSON object; a missing/non-object inputSchema is rejected with a 400 naming the tool.

rules.consequence: Without an object schema OpenAI cannot apply strict structured outputs, and the model has no shape to fill.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI expects an object parameters schema for structured/strict function calling; without one the model lacks a shape to fill and argument quality drops.

rules.consequence: Most providers tolerate a missing schema but the model then has to guess argument shapes.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} tolerates a missing/empty input schema, but the model must guess argument shapes — declare a typed object schema for reliable calls and portability to stricter providers (xAI rejects a non-object root).

tests.user_facing_name: Schema property count within strict-mode limit
tests.what_it_does: Counts total properties across the inputSchema tree against the provider's strict-mode cap (OpenAI: 100 total properties).

applies_to.models_note: OpenAI strict mode. Other providers: advisory only.

verdict_bands.na: provider has no strict-schema property cap

tests.recommendation: Flatten or split the tool; move rarely-used parameters into a nested 'options' object or a second tool. OpenAI strict mode rejects > 100 total properties.

impact.what_happens: Strict-mode providers reject schemas over the property cap; others slow or degrade on huge schemas.

rules.consequence: OpenAI strict mode rejects schemas exceeding 100 object properties.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI strict function schemas reject more than 100 object properties; the call fails until the schema is simplified.

rules.consequence: No strict cap; very large/deep schemas merely degrade selection.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} has no strict 100 object properties cap; oversized schemas degrade accuracy rather than hard-fail.

tests.user_facing_name: Schema nesting depth within strict-mode limit
tests.what_it_does: Measures the maximum object nesting depth of the inputSchema against the provider's strict-mode cap (OpenAI: 5 levels).

applies_to.models_note: OpenAI strict mode. Advisory for others; deeply nested schemas degrade most models.

verdict_bands.na: provider has no strict-schema depth cap

tests.recommendation: Flatten deeply nested objects; reference shared shapes by id rather than inlining several levels deep.

impact.what_happens: Strict-mode providers reject schemas nested beyond the depth cap; others degrade.

rules.consequence: OpenAI strict mode rejects schemas exceeding 5 nesting levels.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI strict function schemas reject more than 5 nesting levels; the call fails until the schema is simplified.

rules.consequence: No strict cap; very large/deep schemas merely degrade selection.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} has no strict 5 nesting levels cap; oversized schemas degrade accuracy rather than hard-fail.

tests.user_facing_name: Schema avoids unsupported keywords
tests.what_it_does: Detects JSON Schema keywords the target model does not support in tool schemas (OpenAI strict: oneOf/$ref disallowed; allOf limited), which cause rejection or silent mishandling.

applies_to.models_note: All providers impose SOME schema-keyword constraints; severity is provider-specific (OpenAI strict hard-rejects; Gemini medium; Anthropic permissive).

verdict_bands.warn: uses keywords supported only in non-strict mode
verdict_bands.fail: uses unsupported keywords for strict/forced mode

tests.recommendation: Rewrite unions as nullable fields or split into separate tools; inline $ref shapes. For OpenAI strict mode, set additionalProperties:false and mark all properties required.

impact.what_happens: Strict/forced modes reject unsupported keywords (oneOf/$ref); elsewhere they may be silently ignored.

rules.consequence: OpenAI strict mode rejects oneOf/$ref and requires additionalProperties:false with all-required.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI strict function schemas reject unsupported keywords (oneOf/$ref); the call fails until the schema is rewritten.

rules.consequence: Gemini 2.5+/3 added anyOf/$ref support, but very large/nested or ANY-mode schemas are still rejected.
rules.rationale_template: Gemini supports more keywords than OpenAI strict but still rejects oversized/forced-mode schemas — usually fixable, occasionally blocking.

rules.consequence: Anthropic accepts a broad JSON-Schema subset; unsupported-keyword risk is mainly portability to stricter models.
rules.rationale_template: Anthropic is permissive about schema keywords, so this is low-impact here — but the same schema may fail on OpenAI.

tests.user_facing_name: Enum value counts are reasonable
tests.what_it_does: Flags very large enums in the schema, which inflate token cost and add latency / can hit provider enum limits.

applies_to.models_note: Soft, all models; OpenAI notes large enums add latency.

tests.recommendation: Replace huge enums with a free-form string plus validation, or fetch the allowed set via a separate lookup tool.

impact.what_happens: Very large enums inflate tokens and add latency, and can hit provider enum limits.

tests.user_facing_name: Single tool definition size
tests.what_it_does: Flags an individual tool whose full definition (name+description+schema) is unusually large, both in absolute tokens and as a share of the window.

applies_to.models_note: All; also expressed as % of window for small-window models.

tests.recommendation: Slim the heaviest tools first — they dominate footprint. Trim schema descriptions, drop redundant examples, and split mega-tools.

impact.what_happens: One oversized tool dominates footprint and, on small windows, can alone threaten overflow.

rules.consequence: On a tiny window a single oversized tool definition is a large share of the budget and can threaten overflow on its own.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window is small; one heavy tool definition is a big fraction of it and can alone push toward overflow.

rules.consequence: A mid window means an oversized tool meaningfully crowds context and is re-sent every call.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window makes a single oversized tool a real drag — it dominates footprint and is paid on every request.

rules.consequence: On a large window one heavy tool is mostly a per-call cost concern, not a fit problem.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window absorbs a heavy tool definition; impact is mainly the per-call cost of re-sending it, but the verdict bands still flag very large tools.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool results fit the result-size limit
tests.what_it_does: On a live call, measures the tool result returned to the model against the documented result-size cap (or a window-share budget), since one chatty tool can blow the window.

threshold.computed: normalize: OpenAI '512KB'->bytes (low conf, Tier-4); M365 '25 items' is an ITEM-count check (not tokens/bytes); otherwise use the window-share fallback (warn 10%, fail 25%).

applies_to.models_note: Documented for M365 Copilot (25 items) / OpenAI (~512 KB); else falls back to a window-share budget (warn 10%, fail 25%).

tests.recommendation: Add pagination/filtering/summarization to chatty tools; cap rows returned. The MCP community is standardizing a client max_response_bytes for exactly this.

impact.what_happens: A large tool result floods the window, truncating context or blowing the budget in one call.

rules.consequence: A result over the documented cap is truncated or rejected by the host/product layer (OpenAI ~512KB; M365 Copilot 25 items).
rules.rationale_template: {provider} caps a single tool result at {tools_mcp.max_tool_result_size}; past it the result is truncated/rejected, so chatty tools must paginate or summarize.

rules.consequence: No documented result cap; a large result instead consumes window share and can flood context in one call.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} documents no per-result size cap, so the budget is window-share against its {context.context_window_tokens}-token window (warn 10% / fail 25%); one chatty tool can still flood context.

tests.user_facing_name: Session stays within the context window
tests.what_it_does: Tracks cumulative tokens (tool definitions + system + conversation + tool results) across a session against the window; trips before the model overflows.

applies_to.models_note: All models; maps to the existing run outcome 'context_overflow'.

tests.recommendation: Reduce tool footprint, trim history, summarize tool results, or move to a larger-window model. Enable prompt caching so the static prefix is cheap to re-send.

impact.what_happens: Cumulative tokens exceed the window; the session truncates history or fails.

rules.consequence: On a tiny window cumulative session tokens hit 100% quickly; the session truncates history or fails outright.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window is small; tool definitions + history + results reach the ceiling fast, so overflow is a hard failure that arrives early.

rules.consequence: Hitting 100% of the window truncates history or fails the run regardless of window size — the high-water gate is a hard limit.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window gives more headroom, but reaching it still truncates history or fails the session — a hard ceiling.

rules.consequence: A large window makes overflow rare, but a long tool-heavy session can still reach it; trim history or summarize before it does.
rules.rationale_template: {provider}'s {context.context_window_tokens}-token window makes overflow unlikely, but a long tool-heavy session can still approach it; the warn band (80%) is the early signal.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool calls per turn within the loop cap
tests.what_it_does: Counts tool-call cycles in a single turn against the model/SDK per-turn or agent-loop cap, beyond which the run is force-stopped.

applies_to.models_note: Binding numbers are host/SDK-level: Anthropic server guardrail ~20 tool calls (pause_turn, non-overridable); OpenAI Agents SDK max_turns=10. Resolve from cross.providers.<provider>.agent_loop_default_turns / cross.sdk_defaults.

tests.recommendation: Break long agentic chains into sub-tasks, raise the SDK max_turns where configurable (not overridable for Anthropic's server guardrail), or reduce required tool hops per task.

impact.what_happens: The model/SDK force-stops the turn once the tool-call cap is hit, leaving the task unfinished.

rules.consequence: Anthropic force-stops the turn after ~20 tool calls (pause_turn), non-overridable.
rules.rationale_template: Anthropic enforces a server-side ~20-tool-call guardrail per turn (pause_turn, cannot be overridden); long chains are cut off.

rules.consequence: OpenAI Agents SDK stops at 10 turns by default (configurable).
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI Agents SDK defaults to max_turns=10 (raise via max_turns); long agentic chains stop unless increased.

tests.user_facing_name: Parallel tool calls within limit
tests.what_it_does: Checks how many tools the model emits in parallel in one turn against any documented parallel-call cap.

applies_to.models_note: Most providers support parallel calls with no fixed numeric cap; NA where unspecified.

tests.recommendation: If a provider caps parallel calls, disable parallel tool use or batch the work; verify the host executes parallel tool results in the order the model expects.

impact.what_happens: Parallel calls beyond a cap are rejected or mis-ordered.

rules.consequence: A documented parallel-call cap is enforced; emitting more (or any, where the cap is 1) is rejected or serialized, breaking parallel workflows.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} caps parallel tool calls at {tools_mcp.max_parallel_tool_calls_count} (M365 Copilot is sequential-only, =1); calls beyond it are rejected or forced sequential — disable parallel tool use or batch the work.

rules.consequence: No fixed numeric cap; parallel calls are generally supported but ordering/host execution can still vary.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} publishes no fixed parallel-call cap; parallel tool use is generally supported, but confirm the host executes results in the order the model expects.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool latency within the host timeout
tests.what_it_does: Compares a tool's measured execution latency against the host's tool-call timeout (e.g. MCP SDK 60s, M365 Copilot 45s); slow tools get cancelled.

applies_to.models_note: Host-level. MCP TS SDK 60s default; M365 45s; Claude Desktop ~60s; configurable in Claude Code.

tests.recommendation: Make long-running tools async (return a job id + poll), stream partial results, or raise the host timeout where configurable.

impact.what_happens: A slow tool exceeds the host timeout and the call is cancelled mid-task.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool prefix is cache-eligible
tests.what_it_does: Checks whether the static prefix (tool definitions + system prompt) is large enough to be cached on this model and would benefit, given the model's prompt-cache minimum and breakpoint rules.

applies_to.models_note: Where prompt caching exists: Anthropic (min 1024, max 4 breakpoints, cached tokens skip rate limit), OpenAI (1024), Gemini (2048/4096). NA where unsupported (Mistral has no caching).

verdict_bands.pass: prefix >= min cacheable AND caching enabled
verdict_bands.warn: prefix below min cacheable (caching won't trigger)

tests.recommendation: Order static content (tools, system) first and place a cache breakpoint after it. On Anthropic, cached tool tokens also stop counting toward your rate limit — a large win for tool-heavy sessions.

impact.what_happens: If the static prefix is below the cache minimum, caching never triggers and full tool cost is paid every call.

rules.consequence: Anthropic caches the tool+system prefix (min 1024 tokens, up to 4 breakpoints); cached tokens are billed at 0.1x AND skip the ITPM rate limit — a large miss if the prefix is below the minimum or unordered.
rules.rationale_template: Anthropic supports prompt caching (min 1024 tokens, 4 breakpoints); cached tool tokens cost 0.1x and do not count toward ITPM — order static content first and add a breakpoint or you pay full tool cost every call.

rules.consequence: OpenAI caches automatically above 1024 tokens; a static prefix below the minimum never caches and pays full cost each call.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI caches prefixes >=1024 tokens automatically; keep the tool+system prefix above the minimum and stable so the cache hits (cached tokens still count toward TPM, unlike Anthropic).

rules.consequence: Gemini supports implicit/explicit caching above 2048/4096 tokens; a smaller prefix won't cache.
rules.rationale_template: Gemini supports prompt caching above its 2048/4096-token minimum; keep the tool+system prefix above it and front-loaded to benefit.

tests.user_facing_name: Estimated cost per task
tests.what_it_does: Estimates the dollar cost of a representative task on this model from observed input/output/cached/reasoning tokens and the model's pricing, so models can be ranked on cost for the same workload.

applies_to.models_note: SaaS with published pricing. Open-weight: cost is self-hosted compute (report tokens, mark price NA).

verdict_bands.warn: above a user-set budget per task

tests.recommendation: Compare cost across models for the same task; remember output is 3-5x input and reasoning tokens bill at output rate. Caching and batch cut input cost 50-90%.

impact.what_happens: The same task costs materially more on a pricier model or token mix.

rules.consequence: Priced per token; rank $/task across models.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} charges {cost.input_per_mtok_usd}/1M input and {cost.output_per_mtok_usd}/1M output; weight output (3-5x) and reasoning tokens for $/task.

rules.consequence: Self-hosted: cost is GPU/compute time — not per-token and not zero.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} is self-hosted: cost is GPU/compute time (not per-token, not free); size for throughput, not a per-token bill.

tests.user_facing_name: Session throughput within rate limits
tests.what_it_does: Estimates whether the session's token rate (including tool definitions re-sent each call) fits the model's tokens-per-minute tier, since big tool sets consume rate-limit quota on every request.

applies_to.models_note: SaaS with TPM tiers. Anthropic note: cached tokens do NOT count toward ITPM, materially changing headroom.

tests.recommendation: Cache the static tool prefix (free of ITPM on Anthropic), raise your tier, or reduce tool-definition tokens re-sent per request.

impact.what_happens: Re-sent tool definitions consume TPM quota, throttling the session.

rules.consequence: Tool definitions are re-sent every call and count toward ITPM — but on Anthropic CACHED tokens do not, so caching the tool prefix materially restores headroom.
rules.rationale_template: Anthropic meters ITPM on UNCACHED input only; re-sent tool definitions burn quota, but caching the tool prefix removes it from the rate limit — a large win for tool-heavy sessions.

rules.consequence: OpenAI meters TPM on input+output and CACHED tokens still count, so re-sent tool definitions consume quota even when cached.
rules.rationale_template: OpenAI counts cached tokens toward TPM, so re-sending tool definitions consumes rate-limit quota on every call; raise your tier or trim tool tokens — caching cuts cost but not TPM.

rules.consequence: A SaaS TPM tier governs sustained throughput; large tool sets re-sent each call eat into it and can throttle the session.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} enforces a per-minute token tier; re-sent tool definitions consume it on every request, so a big tool set can throttle a busy session — cache the prefix or raise the tier.

rules.consequence: Self-hosted open-weight: throughput is bounded by your own GPU/serving capacity, not a provider TPM tier.
rules.rationale_template: {provider} is self-hosted, so there is no provider TPM tier to exceed; throughput is bounded by your serving stack (size for it), not a rate limit.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool annotations are present and self-consistent
tests.what_it_does: Checks the tool declares MCP behavior annotations (readOnlyHint / destructiveHint / idempotentHint / openWorldHint) and that they are internally coherent — e.g. a tool is not both readOnlyHint:true and destructiveHint:true. Hosts use these hints to decide what to auto-run vs confirm.

applies_to.models_note: Design-quality lint; host behavior, not model-specific. From the mcp-builder best-practice guidance.

tests.recommendation: Declare readOnlyHint/destructiveHint/idempotentHint/openWorldHint and keep them consistent: a read-only tool must not also be destructive. Hosts gate auto-execution and confirmation on these hints.

impact.what_happens: Without coherent annotations a host may auto-run a destructive tool, or needlessly gate a safe one, mis-handling the tool.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool name follows a clear naming convention
tests.what_it_does: Checks the tool name reads as a service-prefixed, action-verb, snake_case identifier (e.g. github_create_issue) rather than a bare or ambiguous name. Clear, consistent names measurably improve tool-selection accuracy.

applies_to.models_note: Design-quality lint from the mcp-builder skill; advisory, not model-specific.

verdict_bands.warn: single bare word, non-snake_case, or no action verb

tests.recommendation: Name tools as service_action (snake_case) — e.g. jira_create_ticket, db_run_query. Consistent verb-led, namespaced names cut tool-selection ambiguity, especially in large sets.

impact.what_happens: Ambiguous or inconsistent names make the model pick the wrong tool more often.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool description explains when and how to use it
tests.what_it_does: Heuristically rates description quality beyond mere presence: does it have enough substance and signal when-to-use / examples (cue words, length, multiple sentences) rather than a terse one-liner. Quality descriptions are the strongest lever on selection accuracy.

applies_to.models_note: Design-quality heuristic from the mcp-builder skill; advisory, not model-specific.

tests.recommendation: Describe what the tool does AND when to use it, with a short example or trigger phrases. Distinguish it from sibling tools. This is the single biggest lever on tool-selection accuracy.

impact.what_happens: A thin description leaves the model unsure when to call the tool, raising mis-selection.

tests.user_facing_name: List-style tools support pagination
tests.what_it_does: Detects whether a tool's input schema exposes pagination/limiting controls (limit / offset / page / cursor / page_size / per_page). Tools that can return large lists without a way to cap output flood the context window.

applies_to.models_note: Design-quality lint from the mcp-builder skill; advisory. Most relevant for list/search/query tools.

tests.recommendation: Add limit/offset (or cursor) parameters to any tool that can return a list, and default to a sane page size. Unbounded results are a top cause of context overflow.

impact.what_happens: An unbounded list tool can return a huge result that floods the context window.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool offers a concise/detailed output control
tests.what_it_does: Detects whether the tool's input schema exposes an output-shaping parameter (response_format / detail / verbosity / fields / format / view) that lets the caller request a concise vs full response, keeping token cost down when detail is not needed.

applies_to.models_note: Design-quality lint from the mcp-builder skill; advisory. Most relevant for tools that can return verbose payloads.

verdict_bands.pass: schema exposes a response-format / detail control
verdict_bands.warn: no way to request a concise response (always full payload)

tests.recommendation: Offer a response_format/detail parameter (e.g. concise vs full, or a fields selector) so the model can pull only what it needs and avoid paying for verbose payloads it will not use.

impact.what_happens: Without a concise mode every call returns the full payload, inflating tokens and cost.

tests.user_facing_name: stdio transport is protocol-clean (no stdout contamination)
tests.what_it_does: For stdio servers, checks that the connect + tools/list handshake completed without protocol/parse errors. Logging written to stdout (instead of stderr) corrupts the JSON-RPC stream and shows up as connect/parse failures — observable from the client, no source needed.

applies_to.models_note: Transport-level health check (stdio only); host/transport behavior, not model-specific. Resolves NA in the static heatmap engine, which has no per-connection error stream; surfaced from the scan's connect events.

verdict_bands.fail: protocol/parse errors during connect (likely stdout contamination)
verdict_bands.na: non-stdio transport, or no connect diagnostics available

tests.recommendation: Route all server logging to stderr, never stdout — stdout must carry only JSON-RPC frames. A single stray print corrupts the stream and breaks the connection.

impact.what_happens: stdout contamination corrupts the JSON-RPC frame stream; the client cannot parse responses and the connection fails.

tests.user_facing_name: Tool actually caps/truncates large responses
tests.what_it_does: Executes the tool once on a read-only path and confirms a large response is actually capped/truncated by the tool (e.g. an explicit truncation marker or a bounded size), rather than dumping an unbounded payload into context. Complements the static pagination lint with real behavior.

applies_to.models_note: Single-execution design check (read-only tools only — gate on readOnlyHint/destructiveHint). From the mcp-builder skill. Not part of the static heatmap set.

verdict_bands.pass: response is bounded / explicitly truncated when large
verdict_bands.warn: large response returned with no truncation guard
verdict_bands.na: tool not safely executable (non-read-only) or not exercised

tests.recommendation: Cap response size inside the tool and signal truncation (e.g. a 'truncated: true' marker + a next-cursor), so a single chatty call cannot flood the window even when the caller omits a limit.

impact.what_happens: A tool with no internal cap can return an unbounded payload that floods context in one call.

tests.user_facing_name: Agent completes representative tasks with this server
tests.what_it_does: The end-to-end effectiveness eval: over a set of representative tasks in a monitored multi-turn session, measures how often the agent actually completes the task using the server's tools. This is the mcp-builder agent eval harness and is the real test of whether the surface is usable, not just well-formed.

applies_to.models_note: Live-session effectiveness eval (BACKLOG). Plugs into the live-session monitoring + the mcp-builder eval harness; not part of the static heatmap set.

verdict_bands.na: no eval suite run for this server/model

tests.recommendation: Run a small task suite per server/model and track completion rate. A surface that passes every static lint can still fail in practice — iterate descriptions, tool granularity, and error messages against real failures.

impact.what_happens: A low success rate means the agent cannot reliably accomplish tasks with the server even when every static check passes.
